list.listitem: Brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) is helpful in differentiating acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) from cardiogenic pulmonary edema. C

In patients with indeterminate findings on lung ultrasound, echocardiogram or pulmonary artery catheterization may be required to make the diagnosis of ARDS. Positive lung ultrasound provides strong evidence of ARDS (LR+ 10.8).B

ATS/ESICM/SCCM guidelines recommend 1) mechanical ventilation using lower tidal volumes of 4–8 ml/kg predicted body weight and lower inspiratory pressures with a plateau pressure < 30 cm H2O; 2) prone position >12 hours per day in patients with severe ARDS; A 3) higher PEEP in patients with moderate to severe ARDS; and 4) use of recruitment maneuvers in patients with moderate to severe ARDS.B
A conservative oxygen strategy (target PaO2 55-70 mm Hg) is not more effective, and may be more harmful, than a liberal oxygen strategy (PaO2 90-105 mm Hg).B
There is some evidence that corticosteroids reduce the duration of ventilation and that they may reduce mortality, especially if given in the first 7 days.B
Long-term physical and psychological sequelae are common in both COVID and non-COVID related ARDS. B

background.definition: ARDS is a severe manifestation of acute lung injury (ALI). ALI is defined as a syndrome of acute and persistent lung inflammation with increased vascular permeability.

list.listitem: A prospective multicenter cohort study indicated that ALI was more common than previously thought, with an age-adjusted incidence of 86.2 per 100,000 patient years and a mortality of 38%.
Extrapolation of these data suggests 190,600 cases of ALI per year, associated with 74,000 deaths.
Among ICU patients, 10% to 15% of all patients meet criteria for ARDS, and up to 20% of intubated patients meet criteria for ARDS.
Sepsis (the most common cause of ARDS)
Aspiration of gastric contents
Infectious pneumonia
Severe trauma and surface burns
Massive blood transfusion
Transfusion-related lung injury (TRALI)
Relief of upper airway obstruction
Lung or bone marrow (and stem cell) transplantation
Drug overdose (aspirin, cocaine, opioids, phenothiazines, tricyclic antidepressants)
Idiosyncratic drug reactions (protamine, nitrofurantoin, many chemotherapeutic agents)

The exudative phase is the initial pathologic state, which is characterized by diffuse alveolar damage due to inflammatory injury. This is manifest by proteinaceous fluid in the alveoli and functional loss of surfactant leading to alveolar collapse. The consequences of this lung injury are impaired gas exchange, decreased pulmonary compliance, and pulmonary hypertension.

The proliferative phase occurs over the first week as there is resolution of alveolar edema and the hyperplasia of type II pneumocytes, interstitial myofibroblasts, and deposition of interstitial collagen.
The fibrotic phase is a third phase not seen in all patients and is characterized by disruption of lung architecture, diffuse lung fibrosis, and cyst formation.
Patients with bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and a PaO2/FIO2 ratio of less than 200 mm Hg should be given a test for BNP. C
A BNP of less than 200 makes the diagnosis of ARDS more likely, whereas a BNP of greater than 1200 makes the diagnosis of cardiogenic pulmonary edema more likely. C

BNP levels between 200 and 1200 are not useful in distinguishing between ARDS and cardiogenic pulmonary edema. In this case a transthoracic echocardiogram or pulmonary artery catheter may be required for the diagnosis. C
Lung ultrasound is valuable for ruling in ARDS when positive (LR+ 10.8).B

Differential.Differential_Features: If the BNP is less than 100 (or <200 if the glomerular filtration rate [GFR] is <60 mL/min), congestive heart failure is unlikely.
Bloody fluid is obtained from bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL).
This is a rare, fulminant lung disease that is essentially indistinguishable from ARDS; it occurs in patients most often over fifty with no prior lung disease.
Eosinophils are recovered from BAL, peripheral eosinophilia is inconsistently present, and a dramatic response to corticosteroids is seen.
This is most commonly from leukemia or lymphoma but can also be seen in solid tumors.

list.listitem: ALI is characterized by three clinical features: (1) bilateral radiographic infiltrates; (2) PaO2/FIO2 between 200 and 300 mm Hg regardless of positive end-expiratory pressure (where FIO2 is expressed as between 0.21 and 1.0); and (3) there is no clinical evidence for an elevated left atrial pressure. If measured, the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is less than 18 mm Hg.
The definition of ARDS is the same as that of ALI except that the hypoxia is worse, with a PaO2/FIO2 of 200 mm Hg or less.
Acute onset of dyspnea is the hallmark of ARDS.
Cyanosis is seen if oxygen desaturation is present.

Look for risk factors for ARDS including those producing direct lung injury (ie, aspiration, diffuse pneumonia, toxic gas inhalation) and those conditions associated with indirect injury (sepsis, shock, acute pancreatitis, drug overdose, and severe nonthoracic trauma).

Use the physical examination to help exclude the probability of an ARDS "mimic" such as congestive heart failure (CHF; look for jugular venous distention [JVD], S3, acute heart murmur); however, ancillary diagnostic studies are commonly needed for precise diagnosis.

There is no single "gold standard" diagnostic test for ARDS. Instead, a combination of tests, including clinical impression, CXR, BNP, echocardiography, and occasionally pulmonary artery catheterization has been used to make a diagnosis of ARDS.

In patients with acute respiratory failure and bilateral infiltrates, a very low BNP level helps rule in ARDS (LR = 4.6), and a very high BNP (>1200 pg/mL) makes the diagnosis of cardiogenic pulmonary edema (CPE) more likely (LR = 6.52). Intermediate levels of BNP (200-1200 pg/mL) are not helpful in differentiating ARDS from CPE.

A systematic review of 11 studies with 2648 patients (598 with ARDS) found that lung ultrasound had fair sensitivity (63.1%) and excellent specificity (94.2%) for the diagnosis of ARDS (LR+ 10.9, LR- 0.39). It is therefore more helpful for ruling in ARDS when positive.

Transthoracic echocardiography that shows significant aortic or mitral valve dysfunction or severe left ventricular systolic dysfunction makes CPE a more likely diagnosis than ARDS. However, CPE may be present with normal ventricular function in the setting of acute myocardial ischemia or diastolic dysfunction.

When the diagnosis remains uncertain following clinical evaluation, BNP, and transthoracic echocardiogram, placement of a pulmonary artery catheter is a reasonable option. If the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure is greater than 18 mm Hg, some degree of CPE is present. Interpretation of the pulmonary capillary wedge pressure can be misleading in patients on very high levels of positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP).
If a pulmonary artery catheter is required for diagnostic purposes, it should be removed as soon as feasible.
See algorithm in .

ATS/ESICM/SCCM guidelines recommend (1) mechanical ventilation using lower tidal volumes of 4–8 ml/kg predicted body weight and lower inspiratory pressures with a plateau pressure < 30 cm H2O; (2) prone position >12 hours per day in patients with severe ARDS; A (3) higher PEEP in patients with moderate to severe ARDS; and (4) use of recruitment maneuvers in patients with moderate to severe ARDS.B
High-frequency oscillation and ECMO do not reduce hospital and 30-day mortality due to ARDS compared to conventional mechanical ventilation and are not recommended.B
A conservative oxygen strategy (target PaO2 55-70 mm Hg) is not more effective, and may be more harmful, than a liberal oxygen strategy (PaO2 90-105 mm Hg).B
There is some evidence that corticosteroids reduce the duration of ventilation and that they may reduce mortality, especially if given in the first 7 days.B

An RCT randomized 91 patients with early severe ARDS to methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/d by continuous intravenous infusion or placebo. In the treated patients, 54% were breathing without the ventilator at 7 days compared with 25% of control patients (NNT = 4) and had a lower ICU mortality (20.6% vs. 42.9%; NNT = 5). Prior studies had generally shown no benefit to early or late administration of corticosteroids; however, in these previous studies higher doses of corticosteroids had been used (as high as methylprednisolone 30 mg/kg/d).

The largest trial to date randomized 180 patients with ARDS of at least 7 days duration to methylprednisolone or placebo, and found no effect on mortality and worse long-term outcomes in those randomized more than 14 days after the onset of ARDS.

The Cochrane review found a trend toward lower all-cause mortality at 3 months (RR 0.77, 95% CI 0.57-1.05) based on 6 RCTs with 574 patients. They also found a trend toward reduced duration of ventilation (-4.3 days, 95% CI -9.7 to +1.1 days). Ventilatory free days up to day 28 were significantly reduced with corticosteroids (MD 4.1 days, 95% CI 1.7-6.4 days).

A meta-analysis of 10 RCTS with 692 patients with ARDS found an overall reduction in mortality (OR 0.64, 95% CI 0.43-0.95) with moderate heterogeneity (I2 = 42%). Use of a corticosteroid reduced the mean time of ventilation by 2.7 days (95% CI -3.3 to -2.1 days) with good homogeneity (I2 = 0%). There was evidence of publication bias with regards to the mortality outcome (smaller studies showing higher mortality were missing).
Another meta-analysis of dexamethasone specifically identified 4 RCTs with 702 patients, and found a reduced all-cause mortality with dexamethasone (OR 0.62, 95% CI 0.44 to 0.88).

Convalescent plasma with a neutralizing antibody titer of at least 1:160 administered close to initiation of mechanical ventilation (≤48 hours) decreases 28-day mortality (35.4% vs 45.0%; P = .03; NNT=10) compared to usual care among ICU patients with COVID-19-induced ARDS.

A Cochrane review was unable to draw conclusion regarding the efficacy of n-acetylcysteine, statins, surfactants, or beta-agonists. In each case the confidence interval for mortality was close to 1.0.
A meta-analysis of five RCTs found no mortality benefit to exogenous pulmonary surfactant in adults with ARDS.
A meta-analysis of 12 RCTs with 1237 patients found no benefit to inhaled nitric oxide in ARDS.
An RCT of 540 patients with ARDS found no benefit from simvastatin therapy.
A Cochrane review identified only 2 studies with 81 patients of aerosolized prostacyclins, and was unable to draw conclusions regarding their efficacy.

A systematic review identified 48 studies that evaluated psychological and physical sequelae 3 months to 5 years following hospitalization of 11,693 patients for ARDS (15% with COVID-19).The used the physical compopnent summary score and mental component summary scores of the SF-36. Compared with a normal population, physical component scores were lower at all time points. The same was true for the mental component score. There were no differences between non-COVID and COVID related ARDS sequelae, other than that more anxiety and depression was seen in patients with non-COVID ARDS.

Most patients with ARDS will require mechanical ventilation. Patients with ARDS should be ventilated with lower tidal volumes (6 mg/kg), and end-expiratory plateau pressure should be maintained at 30 cm H2O or less. ("lung protective ventilation strategy").

The American Thoracic Society/European Society of Intensive Care Medicine/Society of Critical Care Medicine guidelines (2017) make the following recommendations:
Strong recommendation for: 1) mechanical ventilation using lower tidal volumes of 4–8 ml/kg predicted body weight and lower inspiratory pressures with a plateau pressure < 30 cm H2O; and 2) prone position is recommended for more than 12 hours per day in patients with severe ARDS. Conditional recommendations are made for the use of 1) higher positive end-experatory pressure (PEEP) in mechanically ventilated patients with moderate to severe ARDS and 2) the use of recruitment maneuvers in patients with moderate to severe ARDS. Recommendation against the routine use of high-frequency oscillatory ventilation in patients with moderate to severe ARDS.

When patients are ventilated with a strategy using low tidal volumes (6 mL/kg) and a goal end-expiratory plateau pressure of 30 cm H2O or less, clinical outcomes are similar whether lower or higher levels of PEEP are used.

A Cochrane review of lung protective ventilation identified 6 trials with 1297 patients and found significant reductions in 28 day mortality (RR 0.74, 95% CI 0.61-0.88) and hospital mortality (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.69-0.92).
A Cochrane review of 10 studies with 3841 participants concluded that high PEEP does not reduce mortality but also does not appear to impact barotrauma. High PEEP does improve oxygenation.

Prone positioning improves oxygenation in most patients with ARDS and was demonstrated in one RCT to reduce 28- and 60-day mortality compared to supine positioning (NNT = 6). A subsequent systematic review confirmed the mortality benefit of prone positioning, espeically for patients with severe hypoxemia.

A network meta-analysis of 10 studies with 812 patients with severe ARDS compared low tidal volumes, moderate tidal volumes, prone ventilation position, and venovenous ECMO. They concluded that prone ventilation and venovenous ECMO were more likely to reduce mortality compared with low and moderate tidal volumes.
A meta-analysis of COVID-19 patients with ARDS found that the prone position significantly improved PaO2/FiO2. This was also the conclusion of an umbrella "review of reviews".
Using lung recruitment maneuvers to titrate positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) increases barotrauma, pneumothorax, and deaths compared with the standard low PEEP strategy.

A Cochrane review of recruitment maneuvers identified a reduction in ICU mortality based on 5 poor quality randomized trials (RR 0.83, 95% CI 0.72-0.97), but no effect on in-hospital mortality, 28 day mortality or barotrauma.
A randomized trial of 71 mechanically ventilated adults conclued that non-sedation was no better than light interrupted sedation.

Several RCTs have addressed the question of liberal vs conservative oxygen strategy. The first studied 205 ventilated patients with ARDS and found that a more conservative oxygen strategy that targeted a PaO2 of 55 mm Hg to 70 mm Hg was no more effective, and may have been more harmful, than a more liberal strategy that targeted a PaO2 of 90 mm Hg to 105 mm Hg. The second randomized 965 mechanically ventilated patients and found that a more conservative oxygen delivery strategy that capped the oxygen saturation as measured by pulse oximetry (SpO2) of 97% had no benefit, except possibly in the subset of patients with hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy.
Another trial randomized 2928 patients with acute hypoxemic respiratory failure to a target of 60 mm Hg or 90 mm Hg.There was no difference in mortality between groups.

A cluster randomized trial in 2541 critically ill adults receiving mechanical ventilation compared a lower oxygen saturation target of 90% (range 88 to 92%) with an intermediate target (94%, range 92 to 96%) or a higher target (98%, range 96 to 100%). There was no difference between groups in the primary outcome of ventilator free days or mortality.
Continuous monitoring by pulmonary artery catheter (PAC) does not improve survival or organ function and is associated with more complications compared with central venous catheter-directed therapy.
Two studies with 401 patients evaluated partial liquid ventilation (PLV) for adults with ARDS and found no net benefit.There was insufficient evidence regarding PLV in children.
Extracorporal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) did not significantly reduce 60-day mortality in a RCT of 249 patients with severe ARDS.

A Cochrane review of 10 RCTs with 1850 patients compared high frequency oscillatory with conventional mechanical ventilation, and found no benefit in terms of mortality. One study found increased mortality in the HFO group.

A randomized trial with 1006 patients with moderate to severe ARDS compared early, continuous neuromuscular blockade with usual care. It was halted early for futility. An expert panel concluded that it should only be considered for patients who require deep sedation to facilitate prone positioning or lung protective ventilation.
Mortality from ARDS has dropped from 67% in 1990 to 25% to 30% at present. B
Most deaths in patients with ARDS are not due to lung disease but are from sepsis and multiple organ system failure. B
Survivors of ARDS may show pulmonary gas exchange abnormalities, neurocognitive abnormalities, and decreased quality of life for at least 2 years after the acute illness. B

Survivors of ARDS from 12 hospitals that participated in the ARDS Network randomized trials had substantial impairments in physical functioning at 6 and 12 months; higher average corticosteroid doses and longer intensive care unit stays were associated with worse outcomes. B

While quality of life was similar for survivors of ECMO versus conventional ventilation, overall rates of disability were high following ECMO with only 49% returning to work and 23% requiring assistance at home. B
A higher lung ultrasound score (0 to 36 points using 12 regions or 0 to 48 points using 16 regions) found an association between higher score on admission and higher in-hospital mortality. B
Long-term physical and psychological sequelae are common in both COVID and non-COVID related ARDS. B
Elevated levels of IL-18 may be associated with worse prognosis for patients with ARDS. B
